title: Cap. 7 Contra Sol. 4: three reasons; Rupertus and Ambrose
pass_a_gloss: I answer: where some Divine fact is established, it is rash (not to say impious) to doubt concerning the equity or fittingness of the same. Now that by Christ's death that pact with the human race has been established, from whose tenor eternal life is promised to any human being under the condition of Faith, has long since been demonstrated by us. Concerning this pact Rupertus, in Genesis book 4, chapter 34: We say a pact many times indeed promised, but once entered, by which alone the enmities which were between God and human beings are loosed, namely the passion of Christ the Son of God. For there without any contradiction the constitution of peace is certain, while God, faith of human beings having been accepted, gives to human beings the same Christ his Son, that they may be saved through him. Concerning this ordination of God therefore, founded in Christ's death and merits, and looking to all and each, there is not to be ambiguity. But that is still called into doubt, whether, this universal pact of giving eternal life to all if they have believed having been posited, God exercises liberty and puts forth special mercy in giving this saving Faith to the elect by which they believe; and that through Christ, and on account of Christ's merits applied to them by a certain peculiar privilege. The matter itself speaks. For we see the elect, and the elect alone, in the event obtain from God persevering and saving faith: But to think so great and such a gift specially gifted to them in another way, or with another regard, than on account of Christ's merits ordained and applied to them by a certain special intention of God, is plainly unlawful. For, as Ambrose piously says, Every gift of grace is in Christ, at that saying of the Apostle, Ephesians 1:3: He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ. These things having been established, although (as I said) it is superfluous to dispute about the fittingness of Divine deeds where the deeds themselves are established, yet, lest any scruple be left, first we say that this special intention of God, according to which he decreed with himself on account of Christ's merits to give the elect the special benefits of efficacious grace and salvation, does not fight with that conditioned pact, Whoever has believed will be saved, but rather is a certain special counsel subordinated to the infallible fulfillment of this universal pact. For those who are committed to their own choice under whatever helps of grace either repel Faith or shake it off. Lest therefore that universal pact should bring the effect of salvation to no one, God by this special and secret intention of his cared that the merit of Christ's death should be applied to some, unto the infallible obtaining of Faith and eternal life. Second, we say that there is nothing unjust or incongruous in that this special intention concerning the efficacious application of Christ's merits puts forth its force in some, not in all; because since Christ's death is a free gift of God expended on the human race, the free distribution and application of the merits overflowing thence ought by every right to depend on the mere will of God. Third, we also add that God, who in the Gospel promised to all and each eternal life on account of Christ's merits if they have believed, yet promised to none of the unbelieving that he would give to him on account of Christ's merits that he should believe infallibly and perseveringly. I ask therefore, From which side does this incongruity turn? Not from the side of believers and the saved: For to give on account of Christ's merits to singular persons what was least singularly promised to them is not of blameworthy injustice, but of goodness to be celebrated. Not from the side of the unbelieving and the lost: For to deny to someone that benefit which it is established you owe him by no account can be judged neither unjust in itself nor incongruous with the highest Divine goodness.
pass_b_english: I answer: once a Divine fact stands, it is rash — not to say impious — to quarrel with its equity or fittingness. We have long shown that by Christ's death that covenant with the human race was fixed, by whose terms eternal life is promised to anyone under the condition of faith. On that covenant Rupert of Deutz (on Genesis 4.34) says: we call it a covenant many times promised but once struck, by which alone the enmities between God and humankind are dissolved — namely the passion of Christ the Son of God. There peace is settled without contradiction when God, receiving human faith, gives people the same Christ his Son that they may be saved through him. So there is no doubt about this Divine ordination, founded in Christ's death and merits and looking to every person. What is still doubted is whether, given this universal covenant of eternal life for all who believe, God may freely show special mercy in giving the elect the saving faith by which they believe — and that through Christ, for his merits applied to them by a peculiar privilege. The fact itself speaks. We see the elect alone, in the outcome, receive from God persevering saving faith. To imagine so great a gift given them in any other way or regard than for Christ's merits, ordained and applied by a special Divine intention, is plainly unlawful. As Ambrose says devoutly, every gift of grace is in Christ — pointing to Ephesians 1:3, He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ. That settled, though it is needless to debate the fittingness of Divine deeds when the deeds themselves are clear, still, to leave no scruple: first, this special intention by which God decreed, for Christ's merits, to give the elect the special benefits of efficacious grace and salvation does not fight the conditioned covenant Whoever believes will be saved; it is rather a special counsel subordinated to that universal covenant's sure fulfillment. Those left to their own choice under any helps of grace either push faith away or shake it off. Lest that universal covenant bring salvation's effect to no one, God by this special and secret intention saw to it that Christ's death-merit would be applied to some for the sure obtaining of faith and eternal life. Second, nothing unjust or incongruous follows if this special intention of efficacious application of Christ's merits puts forth its force in some, not in all: Christ's death is God's free gift to the human race, so free distribution and application of the overflowing merits ought by every right to hang on God's mere will. Third, God, who in the Gospel promised every person eternal life for Christ's merits if they believe, never promised any unbeliever that for those merits he would make him believe surely and perseveringly. So where is the incongruity? Not on the side of believers and the saved: to give singular persons, for Christ's merits, what was never singularly promised them is not blameworthy injustice but goodness to praise. Not on the side of the unbelieving and lost: to deny someone a benefit you owe him by no title is neither unjust in itself nor unfit for God's highest goodness.
source_text: Respondeo, ubi de facto aliquo Divino constat, temerarium est (ne dicam impium) de aequitate aut congruitate ejusdem dubitare. Jam vero Christi morte esse stabilitum illud pactum cum humano genere, ex cujus tenore vita aeterna cuivis homini sub Fidei conditione promittitur, jam pridem a nobis demonstratum est. De hoc pacto Rupertus, in 4. Genes. cap. 34, Dicimus pactum multoties quidem promissum, sed semel initum, quo solo inimicitiae solvuntur, quae erant inter Deum & homines, passio scilicet Christi Filii Dei. Illic enim absque ulla contradictione certa est constitutio pacis, dum accepta Deus Fide hominum dat hominibus eundem Christum Filium suum, ut salventur per ipsum. De hac itaque Dei ordinatione in Christi morte meritisque fundata, atque ad omnes & singulos spectante, non est ambigendum. Verum illud adhuc in dubium vocatur, utrum posito hoc universali pacto dandae vitae aeternae omnibus, si crediderint, Deus exerceat libertatem, & exserat specialem misericordiam in danda hac Fide salutifera electis qua credant; idque per Christum, & propter merita Christi peculiari quodam privilegio ad eos applicata. Res ipsa loquitur. Videmus enim electos, & solos electos, in eventu obtinere a Deo fidem perseverantem & salutiferam: Putare autem tantum ac tale donum illis specialiter donatum alio modo, aut intuitu quam propter merita Christi illis speciali quadam intentione Dei ordinata & applicata, plane nefas est. Nam, ut pie Ambrosius, Omne donum gratiae in Christo est, ad illud Apostoli, Ephes. i. 3. Benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in Christo. Hisce constitutis, quamvis (ut dixi) supervacaneum est de congruitate Divinorum factorum disceptare ubi de ipsis factis constat, tamen, ne quid scrupuli relinquatur, primo dicimus, Hanc specialem Dei intentionem, juxta quam apud se decrevit propter merita Christi dare electis specialia beneficia gratiae efficacis & salutis, non pugnare cum pacto illo conditionato, Quisquis crediderit salvus erit, sed potius esse speciale quoddam consilium, ad universalis hujus pacti infallibilem impletionem subordinatum. Qui enim suo arbitrio committuntur sub quibusvis gratiae adminiculis, aut Fidem repellunt, aut excutiunt. Ne itaque pactum illud universale nemini effectum salutis apportaret, Deus speciali hac & arcana sua intentione curavit aliquibus applicatum iri mortis Christi meritum, ad Fidei vitaeque aeternae infallibilem consecutionem. Secundo, dicimus, Nihil iniqui aut incongrui esse, quod haec specialis intentio de efficaci applicatione meritorum Christi in aliquibus, non in omnibus vim suam exserat; quia cum mors Christi sit gratuitum Dei donum humano generi impensum, libera distributio & applicatio meritorum inde redundantium omni jure ex mera Dei voluntate dependere debeat. Tertio, & illud addimus, Deum, qui in Evangelio promisit omnibus & singulis vitam aeternam propter merita Christi, si crediderint, nulli tamen infidelium promisisse se illi propter merita Christi daturum ut infallibiliter & perseveranter credat. Quaero igitur, Ex qua parte versatur haec incongruitas? Non ex parte credentium & servatorum: Nam dare propter merita Christi singularibus personis quod illis singulariter minime promissum fuit, non est culpandae iniquitatis, sed celebrandae bonitatis. Non ex parte incredulorum & perditorum: Nam illud beneficium negare alicui, quod constat te nulla ratione illi debere, nec in se iniquum, nec summae bonitati Divinae incongruum judicari potest.
